cues.text: Section two is about IT operations: keeping the business running.
IT operations, often shortened to ITOps, comprises the activities that operate and maintain technology infrastructure and services.
Consider a banking application.
It is not useful simply because its code compiles.
Customers need it to remain accessible, secure and responsive, while transactions are processed accurately.
So what does operations include?
It covers server and cloud administration, network management, database maintenance, storage, monitoring, patching, backup, incident response, capacity planning and end-user support.
Notice that it combines people, processes and technology.
Now let us separate three levels of thinking.
Strategic IT determines the long-term direction: what capabilities the organisation needs, and why.
Operational IT delivers and sustains those capabilities every day.
For example, a telecom company's decision to expand mobile broadband is strategic.
Monitoring network congestion, repairing equipment and managing capacity are operational.
Between the two sits tactical planning, which connects them by allocating resources and scheduling improvements.
The table that follows compares strategic and operational work across three activities.
I will read it row by row.
First row, cloud.
At the strategic level, the organisation decides its migration objectives and its investment.
At the operational level, it monitors workloads and optimises capacity.
Second row, security.
Strategically, the organisation defines its risk appetite and its security policy.
Operationally, it patches systems and investigates alerts.
Third row, customer service.
Strategically, it defines the desired digital experience.
Operationally, it resolves incidents and monitors latency.
Across all three rows, the pattern is the same: strategy sets the intent and the direction, and operations carries it out day after day.
Next, consider the wider digital ecosystem.
Services depend on partners, APIs, cloud platforms, payment networks and users.
An outage at a payment processor may affect multiple merchants even when their own servers are healthy.
Operations must therefore monitor dependencies, coordinate suppliers, enforce interoperability and maintain fallback arrangements.
This brings us to observability.
Observability helps operators understand system behaviour through metrics, logs and traces.
Metrics quantify behaviour.
Logs record events.
Traces follow requests across components.
There is an important distinction here: monitoring detects known conditions, whereas observability supports investigation of unfamiliar failures.
Finally, automation.
Automation reduces repetitive work, but automated mistakes can spread quickly.
To manage that risk, use tested configuration, review, access controls, rollback and monitoring.
And in the Nigerian context, unreliable electricity and connectivity require practical resilience measures, such as redundant links, backup power and offline-capable workflows.
